title: Purim: Esther
hook: a queen, a villain and a hidden God whose name never appears in the book

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu BiShvat, the new year for trees. Your line was a birthday for trees. Did you stop at one? Now, a month on in the calendar, a story read from a scroll. Day one hundred thirty-three.

Here's a story with everything. A king of Persia who throws a party for half a year. A queen who refuses his summons and is sent away. A beauty contest across the empire, won by a young Jewish woman who keeps her background secret, on her cousin's advice. A proud official who demands everyone bow to him, and when one Jew won't, plots to wipe out every Jew in the kingdom, and casts lots to pick the day. A sleepless king, a banquet, a sudden reversal. It reads like a palace thriller. And in the whole book, one name never appears.
screen: `A KING, A QUEEN, A SECRET.` → `A PLOT, AND LOTS CAST FOR A DAY.` → `ONE NAME NEVER APPEARS.`

segments.voice: The book is Esther, and on Purim it's read aloud from a handwritten scroll called the megillah. Megillah just means scroll, from a root meaning to roll. Purim means lots, the lots Haman cast to choose the day of destruction. And the name that never appears is God's. Not once, in the whole book. There are no miracles, no prophets, no voice from heaven. There's a queen who has to decide whether to risk her life by walking in to the king uninvited, and a cousin, Mordecai, who tells her that if she stays silent, help will come from somewhere else, and adds: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?" She goes in. Everything turns. The Talmud plays on this. It hears in the name Esther the Hebrew for hidden, and they linked her to a verse in Deuteronomy where God says: "And I will surely hide My face in that day." So the book of Esther becomes the story of a hidden God. Not absent, hidden. Working through coincidences, a king's insomnia, a brave woman's choice. Some readers find ordinary life in this: no parted seas, just timing and courage, and, looking back, a pattern. One reason people give for Purim's costumes and masks: they hide who's underneath, the way God is hidden in the story. And look at this week: a hut of branches, four kinds bound together, dancing with the scrolls, lights in the window, a count going up, a tree's birthday, and now a hidden name.
screen: `MEGILLAH: A SCROLL.` · `GOD'S NAME NEVER APPEARS.` · `FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.` · `ESTHER: HIDDEN.` · then, large: `HIDDEN, NOT ABSENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for help that doesn't announce itself. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last year. Was there a moment where something turned out right, and at the time it just looked like luck? A call at the right moment. A stranger. A delay that saved you. Pick one. Replay it slowly. You don't have to decide what it was. Just notice that it was there. The bell holds the time.
Megillah. A scroll, and on Purim, the scroll of Esther, read aloud: a story where God's name never appears.
Your line: hidden, not absent. Today, when something small goes right, pause and wonder who or what was behind it. Day one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: On Purim, Jews hear the book of Esther read aloud from a handwritten scroll, the megillah, both in the evening and again the next morning, often in costume.
